Young also expected European de jure recognition of Lithuania soon, because armed conflict between Poland and Lithuania no longer seemed likely.

output.answer: On 28 February 1924 Curzon told the Lords that Mosul was a question of enormous importance to the Turks. He said it mattered to Britain because of its necessity to the mandated territory of Iraq. Rather than fighting it out at Lausanne, even though it had been discussed at the table, the parties agreed to remit it to negotiations between Britain and Turkey, which were about to begin at Constantinople. If those failed, the Treaty provided for reference to the League of Nations. His remarks give this as the course taken instead of seeking a solution at Lausanne. They do not give any further reason for the remission.

claims.claim: Instead of settling it at Lausanne, it was remitted to Anglo-Turkish negotiations at Constantinople, with League of Nations reference if they failed.

output.answer: Cecil defended the decision chiefly by stressing the care and process behind it, and by justifying its terms. He said it would be impossible to press the Government to reject a decision reached with such immense care: a qualified Commission (a Swede, a Hungarian and a Belgian) investigated, then a Council sub-committee heard both Turkey and Britain. The question of the Council's function was referred to the International Court, whose opinion was that the Council had to give a decision, not merely a recommendation, and the Council adopted it. He also defended the substance: the Council upheld the broad Branting line, subject to delimitation, and made it non-definitive until a fresh treaty extended the Mandate for up to twenty-five years. He presented this as unsurprising in light of Article 22.

MacDonald opposed extending Britain's responsibility for Iraq. He argued that the 1922 Treaty's military and financial commitments should run out by 1928, as it provided. He said that success as Mandatory would let Britain ask the League to admit Iraq by then.

In the evidence, the main reason given is from Mr. Thurtle. He argued that oil "loom[ed] very largely" in the Iraq question. He cited a Daily Telegraph diplomatic correspondent, who reported heavy lobbying by oil interests in the lobbies of Geneva. Mr. Amery rejected the suspicion and said oil had not influenced British policy at all. The evidence gives no wider set of reasons from other critics.

According to Chamberlain, the 1925 proposal was a bargain made outside the League of Nations. Turkey would receive as much of the Mosul vilayet as it wanted, roughly two-thirds. In return, a British company approved by the British Government would get the exploitation of all the oil. The economic motive was therefore control of the region's oil. Chamberlain also denied that Britain was actuated by a desire to secure Iraq's oil.

output.answer: The evidence does not explain why the League failed to remove Poland from Vilna. Lloyd George's speech (chunk 1) says that General Zeligowski defied the League's line and annexed Vilna. It says the League unanimously passed a resolution condemning the act, and that Poland first disowned the general and later honoured him. It does not discuss League enforcement, or why the League could not reverse the annexation. The other chunks are only questions asked in Parliament, with no answers.

The evidence covers only one episode, the Commons debate of 23 March 1926 on the Geneva Council negotiations. In that debate the Opposition attacked the Foreign Secretary rather than the League. Mr. MacDonald called the outcome a lamentable failure of British diplomacy. Mr. Thurtle said Chamberlain had misled the House and had not carried out the wishes of the people. Chamberlain told the House the decision was theirs and that he would not complain if it went against him. The evidence does not show how Parliament reacted to other League decisions.

The evidence does not cover fighting on the Greek-Bulgarian border. The closest chunk is Lord Cecil's April 1924 speech. It says warlike developments ceased "instantly" once the Greeks placed a matter in the League's hands, but it appears to concern a dispute involving a great Power, not a Greek-Bulgarian border clash. The other chunks cover refugee loans, Albania and Bulgarian disarmament. None gives the timing or the reasons for League action on a Greek-Bulgarian border incident.

The evidence doesn't address League sanctions on Italy over Abyssinia. The chunks are 1926 Commons debates on the Anglo-Iraq Treaty, Locarno and League membership, and they say nothing about an Abyssinia dispute or any sanctions imposed on Italy.

The evidence gives British speakers' views, not a full account. In 1926 Sir Alfred Hopkinson said that, on the highest American authority, Clause 10 of the Covenant more than anything else kept the US out. He linked this to American fears that Clause 10 could commit members to armed force in disputes, including on the American continent. In 1920 Lord Sydenham added that the American people were sharply divided and that the US would not join unless the Covenant was modified.

The evidence chunks don't mention the 1938 Munich Conference. They cover 1920s matters (Vilna and the Ambassadors' Conference, a 1920 financial conference, and the 1924 Anglo-French and reparations conferences), so they can't answer what was decided at Munich.

The evidence doesn't say when Germany left the League of Nations. The chunks are all from March 1926 and concern Germany's attempted entry and the dispute over a permanent Council seat. They say nothing about a German withdrawal.

Assuming "there" means the March 1926 failure at Geneva over Germany's entry, the evidence gives critics' explanations, not a neutral verdict. Lord Parmoor blamed the non-use and disregard of the League's Council and Assembly machinery. Sir J. Simon said the Assembly was only used to pass resolutions the Locarno Powers had already prepared, which was not real use of the League machinery. Mr. MacDonald blamed the Foreign Secretary's handling, saying he raised expectations that confused the German issue.
